e.etymology: The English word, from Latin victoria. As a name it spiked in 1918 with the end of World War I and is now used alongside Victoria and Victor.
A Spanish-style spelling of Naomi, from Hebrew Noomi, 'pleasantness'. In the Book of Ruth, Naomi is Ruth's mother-in-law.
A spelling of Delaney, from the Irish surname O Dubhshlaine, built on dubh, 'dark', and a second element linked to the River Slaney. A Norman name meaning 'from the alder grove' merged with it.
From Arabic razan, 'composed, dignified', said of a woman of calm good judgment.
The Spanish phrase mi amor, 'my love', written as one word. It is a recent American coinage, not a traditional Spanish given name.

assoc.t: mi amor, the everyday Spanish endearment 'my love'

e.note: To Spanish speakers it is an everyday endearment for partners and children, not a name.

e.etymology: A recent name used mainly by Pakistani and other South Asian Muslim families. Its derivation is not well documented.
From French Jeannette, a diminutive of Jeanne, the feminine of Jean (John), from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'. In English it was at first chiefly Scottish.
namesakes: Jeanette MacDonald (1930s Hollywood singer and actress)
Jeanette Miller (the Chipette in Alvin and the Chipmunks)

e.etymology: A form of Imogen, first used by Shakespeare in Cymbeline, apparently a misprint for Innogen, from Gaelic inghean, 'girl, maiden'. The -e spelling was the usual American one.
namesakes: Imogene Coca (comedian, Your Show of Shows)
Imogene Herdman (The Best Christmas Pageant Ever)

e.etymology: From Arabic Anisa, 'friendly, good company'. In the US it rose around 1970 with child actress Anissa Jones of the sitcom Family Affair.
namesakes: Anissa Jones (child actress, Buffy on Family Affair)

e.etymology: An older Spanish spelling of Esteban, the Spanish form of Stephen, from Greek stephanos, 'crown, garland'. Saint Stephen was the first Christian martyr.
The Spanish and Portuguese form of Eleanor, from Old Occitan Alienor, a name of uncertain meaning made famous by Eleanor of Aquitaine. The heir to the Spanish throne is Princess Leonor.
namesakes: Leonor, Princess of Asturias (heir to the Spanish throne)

e.etymology: From Old French Ameline, brought to England by the Normans, a pet form of Germanic names in amal, 'work, vigor'. Despite the look, it is not related to Emily.
The Latinate feminine of Philip, from Greek Philippos: philein, 'to love', plus hippos, 'horse'. Medieval English records wrote Philippa for women who were called Philip in speech.
namesakes: Philippa Gregory (author of The Other Boleyn Girl)
Pippa Middleton (born Philippa, sister of Catherine, Princess of Wales)

e.etymology: The Arabic form of Job, the prophet known in both the Bible and the Quran for patience under suffering. Arabic tradition links the name to a root meaning 'to return' to God.
The Arabic form of Canaan, the biblical land and the grandson of Noah it was named for; it is a common Lebanese surname. In the US it also overlaps with Kanan and Canaan as given names.

assoc.t: sounds like Canaan, the biblical Promised Land

e.meaning: mythical firebird reborn from its ashes
e.etymology: A respelling of Phoenix, from Greek phoinix, the legendary bird that burns and rises again from its own ashes. The same Greek word also meant 'crimson'.
A K spelling of Carissa, usually traced to Latin carissima, 'dearest', and influenced by Charissa, a name from Greek charis, 'grace', used by the poet Edmund Spenser.
A short form of names ending in -nella, such as Antonella, Petronella and Fenella, and of Cornelia. It also serves as a Latinate form of Nell, itself from Eleanor, Ellen or Helen.
The Polish pet form of Anna, from Hebrew Channah, 'grace'. In the US it is also used as a spelling of Anya or Aniya.
The name of the Lakota people of the northern Great Plains, from Lakhota, 'allies' or 'friends', a cousin of the word Dakota. It is a nation's name, not a traditional Lakota given name.

assoc.t: the Lakota, a Native American nation of the Great Plains

e.note: The name of a living Native nation; using tribal names as baby names is criticized by some.

e.etymology: A spelling of Dani or Danny, pet forms of Danielle, Daniela and Daniel, from Hebrew Daniyyel, 'God is my judge'.
From Hebrew Yokheved, 'the Lord is glory'. In Exodus she is the mother of Moses, Aaron and Miriam; English Bibles spell the name Jochebed.
From Arabic abbas, 'one who frowns', a byname of the lion. Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib was the Prophet Muhammad's uncle, and Abbas ibn Ali is revered by Shia Muslims as a hero of Karbala.
From Arabic jawad, 'generous, open-handed'. Muhammad al-Jawad, 'the Generous', was the ninth imam of Twelver Shia Islam.
A respelling of Zion, from Hebrew Tsiyon, the hill of Jerusalem where David's city stood, later a name for Jerusalem and for a promised land.

assoc.t: Zion National Park in Utah (same sound)

e.etymology: Most often a phonetic spelling of Gianna, the Italian short form of Giovanna, from Latin Iohanna and Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
From Hebrew Yoach, 'the Lord is brother', the name of several minor Old Testament figures, among them a court recorder under King Hezekiah.
A form of Rosalind, a Germanic name from hros, 'horse', and lind, 'gentle', long reread as Latin rosa linda, 'lovely rose'. Shakespeare used Rosaline in Romeo and Juliet and Love's Labour's Lost.
namesakes: Rosaline (Romeo's first love in Romeo and Juliet)

e.etymology: A respelling of Justice, the English word, from Latin iustitia. Justice was a surname for a judge before it became a virtue name.
From Sanskrit Om, also written Aum, the sacred sound chanted at the start of Hindu prayers and mantras and held to be the sound of the universe itself.

assoc.t: om, the chant used in yoga and meditation
sounds like ohm, the unit of electrical resistance

e.etymology: From the English word for the metal, Old English seolfor, or from the surname Silver, given to a silversmith or to someone with silvery hair.

assoc.t: silver, the metal and the color
Silver, the Lone Ranger's horse (Hi-yo, Silver!)
Long John Silver, the pirate of Treasure Island

e.etymology: A modern American combination of Rae and Lee, also heard as a respelling of Rayleigh.
